issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a trauma type of trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient also directly sustained major physical injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoidance of medical cues can fit some trauma-to-a-loved-one cases, but in this profile it appears to be driven by a personal bodily injury/medical trauma theme that is otherwise unsupported except by the implausible physical-vulnerability appraisal, making this item clinically incoherent with the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Sister Margaret's Vigil

Sister Margaret was fifty-five years old when her younger brother Thomas died in a single-vehicle collision on Route 9 near the convent in upstate New York where she had lived for thirty-two years. It was a Tuesday in March, late afternoon, when the state police arrived at the gatehouse. Thomas had been driving home from work-he was a carpenter, lived forty minutes away in the valley-and had crossed the centerline on a curve that Margaret knew well from her walks along the monastery grounds. The officer said Thomas had been alone in the vehicle. No other cars were involved. The officer did not say it was raining, but Margaret had come to believe it was, though when she reviewed the weather records later, the afternoon had been clear. What she could not reconstruct was why Thomas had been on that particular road that day, or whether he had called her that morning-she had a memory of her phone ringing during lauds, and a memory of not answering it, and these two memories had fused into a single, unbearable certainty: that Thomas had needed her, and she had chosen prayer over picking up the phone.

In the weeks after the funeral, Margaret found herself unable to walk the perimeter path that led toward Route 9. The path curved through the woods behind the refectory, and at a certain point, if you climbed slightly, you could see the road in the distance. She began taking her evening walks in the opposite direction, through the cloister garden, then through the chapel wing-longer routes, circuitous ones. When Sister Judith asked her why she no longer joined the group walk on Thursdays, Margaret said her knees were troubling her, which was not entirely untrue. What was true, and what she could not say, was that the sight of that curve of asphalt, even from a distance, brought the moment flooding back with such force that her hands went numb and her breath came shallow. She would see the road, and then she would see Thomas's hands on the steering wheel-she had never actually seen them, but in the memory they were there, gripping, and then releasing-and the clarity of it was absolute. Some moments in the sequence were vivid: the angle of the afternoon light, the sound of the officer's voice in the parlor. Other moments were gone entirely. She could not remember what she had been wearing when they told her. She could not remember if she had cried.

At night, she began performing small rituals. Before sleep, she would recite a particular Psalm three times-not the usual evening office, but a specific one she had chosen-and then touch the wooden cross that hung above her bed, and then recite it again. If she skipped this, or if she lost count, she would have to begin again. She understood, in the part of her mind that still observed herself, that she was trying to prevent something. She was not certain what. Another death, perhaps. A punishment for her negligence. A sign that God had turned away. The rituals felt necessary in the way that breathing was necessary, and when she performed them, there was a brief moment-never more than a moment-when the weight in her chest lifted slightly.

By autumn, nearly seven months after Thomas's death, Margaret had withdrawn from most of her duties in the community. She had been the librarian for twenty years, but she found that she could not enter the library without becoming overwhelmed by the memory of Thomas visiting once, years ago, running his fingers along the spines of books in the theology section. She requested a transfer to kitchen work, something solitary. The abbess, concerned, suggested that Margaret speak with their spiritual director, but Margaret could not articulate what she would say. How could she explain that she had failed at the most fundamental task of a sister-to love, to pray for, to protect those entrusted to her care? That she had heard her brother calling and had chosen silence? That every day she performed small, private acts of penance, hoping that if she was vigilant enough, if she was punished enough, God would not take anyone else from her?

Her husband of thirty-four years-she had married before entering the convent, a choice the Church had allowed because of her age and circumstances-called her last month. He said she sounded different. Distant. He asked if she was well. Margaret could not tell him that she no longer answered the phone unless she had performed her evening ritual first. She could not tell him that she was terrified of losing him too, and that the only way she knew to prevent that was to remain vigilant, to atone, to never again miss a call. It was this conversation that finally moved her to reach out to a therapist outside the community-someone who might help her understand why she could not stop believing that Thomas's death was her fault, and why the only thing that seemed to quiet the fear was to keep performing the same small acts, over and over, in the dark.
